phrases.translation: Alif-Lãm-Ra. These are the verses of the clear Book
phrases.explanation: The surah opens with the separated letters Alif-Lãm-Ra, whose full meaning is not explained here. They introduce the verses of a clear Book and invite attention to the revelation that follows. The Quran is described as clear. The story that follows is part of its guidance, carrying lessons rather than being told only for entertainment.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Quran so that you may understand
phrases.explanation: The Quran is sent down in Arabic so its first hearers can understand its message. The verse connects revelation with a language accessible to the community receiving it. The purpose is understanding. Hearing the words is not enough by itself. People are invited to reflect on their meaning and guidance.

phrases.translation: We relate to you ˹O Prophet˺ the best of stories through Our revelation of this Quran, though before this you were totally unaware ˹of them˺
phrases.explanation: The account of Joseph is called the best of stories and is conveyed through revelation. Its events offer moral and spiritual lessons rather than a tale invented for amusement. Before the Quran, the Prophet was unaware of this account. The verse emphasizes that he receives the story through revelation, not from earlier personal knowledge.

phrases.translation: ˹Remember˺ when Joseph said to his father, “O my dear father! Indeed I dreamt of eleven stars, and the sun, and the moon—I saw them prostrating to me!”
phrases.explanation: Joseph tells his father about a dream in which eleven stars, the sun, and the moon prostrate to him. The unusual image becomes an early sign in a story whose meaning unfolds over time.

phrases.translation: He replied, “O my dear son! Do not relate your vision to your brothers, or they will devise a plot against you. Surely Satan is a sworn enemy to humankind
phrases.explanation: Jacob warns Joseph not to tell the dream to his brothers. The advice recognizes that a striking vision could deepen jealousy among people already competing for their father’s affection. Jacob fears the brothers may plot against Joseph. His warning is protective, not a claim that the dream itself is harmful. Satan is described as a clear enemy to humanity. The verse connects jealousy and plotting with a broader temptation toward harm.

phrases.translation: And so will your Lord choose you ˹O Joseph˺, and teach you the interpretation of dreams,
phrases.explanation: Jacob tells Joseph that Allah will choose him and teach him to interpret dreams. The ability is presented as a gift from Allah, not merely a skill Joseph acquires by himself.

phrases.translation: and perfect His favour upon you and the descendants of Jacob—˹just˺ as He once perfected it upon your forefathers, Abraham and Isaac. Surely your Lord is All-Knowing, All-Wise.”
phrases.explanation: Allah will complete His favor upon Joseph and the descendants of Jacob. The promise places Joseph’s future within a wider family history of guidance. The favor is compared with what Allah gave Abraham and Isaac. Jacob closes by affirming that Allah knows fully and acts with wisdom.

phrases.translation: Indeed, in the story of Joseph and his brothers there are lessons for all who ask
phrases.explanation: The story of Joseph and his brothers contains lessons for those who ask. The narrative invites reflection on family conflict, patience, trust, and how events can unfold beyond what people expect.

phrases.translation: ˹Remember˺ when they said ˹to one another˺, “Surely Joseph and his brother ˹Benjamin˺ are more beloved to our father than we, even though we are a group of so many. Indeed, our father is clearly mistaken
phrases.explanation: Joseph and Benjamin’s brothers believe their father loves the two younger sons more. Their perception fuels jealousy, even though it does not establish that Jacob is actually unjust. The brothers emphasize that they are the larger group. They measure their importance by numbers and expect that to outweigh their younger siblings’ place in their father’s heart. They accuse their father of being clearly mistaken. The charge reveals how resentment shapes their judgment of Jacob and prepares them to justify a harmful plan.

phrases.translation: Kill Joseph or cast him out to some ˹distant˺ land so that our father’s attention will be only ours, then after that you may ˹repent and˺ become righteous people!”
phrases.explanation: The brothers consider killing Joseph or casting him into a distant land. Their plan is driven by jealousy and treats their brother as an obstacle to remove. They hope their father’s attention will then belong only to them. Their reasoning seeks affection through eliminating a rival rather than repairing the family relationship. They imagine they can repent and become righteous afterward. The plan wrongly treats later repentance as permission to commit a grave harm now.

phrases.translation: One of them said, “Do not kill Joseph. But if you must do something, throw him into the bottom of a well so perhaps he may be picked up by some travellers.”
phrases.explanation: One brother argues against killing Joseph and suggests leaving him in a well where travelers may find him. His proposal is less violent than the others’ plan, but it still abandons Joseph to danger for the sake of their scheme.

phrases.translation: They said, “O our father! Why do you not trust us with Joseph, although we truly wish him well
phrases.explanation: The brothers ask Jacob why he will not trust them with Joseph and claim that they wish him well. Their words conceal the jealousy described in the preceding verses. The question is meant to persuade their father to let Joseph go with them. Their appeal to trust contrasts sharply with what they intend to do.

phrases.translation: Send him out with us tomorrow so that he may enjoy himself and play. And we will really watch over him.”
phrases.explanation: The brothers promise that Joseph will enjoy himself and play if he goes with them. The offer makes the outing sound harmless and attractive to their father. They also promise to watch over Joseph. The assurance is deceptive, because their actual plan is to abandon him in a well.

phrases.translation: He responded, “It would truly sadden me if you took him away with you, and I fear that a wolf may devour him while you are negligent of him.”
phrases.explanation: Jacob says it would sadden him to let Joseph go and fears a wolf could devour him while the brothers are distracted. His concern shows his care for Joseph and his awareness of the risks of the journey.

phrases.translation: They said, “If a wolf were to devour him, despite our strong group, then we would certainly be losers!”
phrases.explanation: The brothers insist that they would be losers if a wolf took Joseph while they were a strong group. Their confidence is a persuasive promise, but it does not reflect their hidden intention.

phrases.translation: And so, when they took him away and decided to throw him into the bottom of the well, We inspired him:
phrases.explanation: The brothers take Joseph away and decide to throw him into a well. Their action turns the jealousy they discussed into a real betrayal of their younger brother. Allah inspires Joseph while he is in the well. The reassurance comes at the moment he is most vulnerable, when his brothers have left him behind.

phrases.translation: “˹One day˺ you will remind them of this deed of theirs while they are unaware ˹of who you are˺.”
phrases.explanation: Joseph is told that one day he will remind them of what they did while they do not recognize him. The promise points to a future reversal beyond what the brothers can foresee.

phrases.translation: Then they returned to their father in the evening, weeping
phrases.explanation: The brothers return to Jacob in the evening, weeping. Their display of grief is part of their attempt to make the false story about Joseph seem believable. The tears are part of their attempt to support the story.

phrases.translation: They cried, “Our father! We went racing and left Joseph with our belongings, and a wolf devoured him! But you will not believe us, no matter how truthful we are.”
phrases.explanation: The brothers claim they were racing and left Joseph with their belongings. Their explanation presents his absence as an accident caused by their play. They say a wolf devoured Joseph and insist that Jacob will not believe them even though they are truthful. The claim anticipates his suspicion while concealing their own responsibility.

phrases.translation: And they brought his shirt, stained with false blood. He responded, “No! Your souls must have tempted you to do something ˹evil˺. So ˹I can only endure with˺ beautiful patience! It is Allah’s help that I seek to bear your claims.”
phrases.explanation: The brothers bring a shirt marked with false blood to support their story. The evidence is fabricated, and Jacob sees that appearances do not make their account true. Jacob says his soul has tempted the brothers to do evil and chooses beautiful patience. He does not deny his grief, but refuses to answer deceit with despair or wrongdoing. Jacob seeks Allah’s help in bearing their claims. His patience is rooted in reliance on Allah, not in indifference to Joseph’s fate.

phrases.translation: And there came some travellers, and they sent their water-boy who let down his bucket into the well. He cried out, “Oh, what a great find! Here is a boy!” And they took him secretly ˹to be sold˺ as merchandise, but Allah is All-Knowing of what they did
phrases.explanation: Travelers arrive and send their water-carrier to lower a bucket into the well. The ordinary act of drawing water unexpectedly reveals the child hidden below. The water-carrier calls out when he finds Joseph. The travelers then secretly take him as merchandise, treating a person as something to sell. Allah knows what the travelers do. Their secrecy cannot hide the injustice from Him, even though Joseph’s future remains unknown to them.

phrases.translation: They ˹later˺ sold him for a cheap price, just a few silver coins—only wanting to get rid of him
phrases.explanation: Joseph is sold for only a few silver coins because the travelers want to get rid of him. The cheap price shows how little they value the child, though Allah’s knowledge of the story’s outcome is greater than theirs.

phrases.translation: The man from Egypt who bought him said to his wife, “Take good care of him, perhaps he may be useful to us or we may adopt him as a son.”
phrases.explanation: The Egyptian buyer tells his wife to care for Joseph and imagines that the boy may help them or become a son. Joseph’s situation appears settled, though his future will be shaped by Allah beyond what the buyer expects.

phrases.translation: This is how We established Joseph in the land,
phrases.explanation: Allah establishes Joseph in the land. The verse frames his new position as part of a divine plan rather than a result controlled only by the people who bought him.

phrases.translation: so that We might teach him the interpretation of dreams. Allah’s Will always prevails, but most people do not know
phrases.explanation: Joseph’s circumstances will allow Allah to teach him the interpretation of dreams. The ability that first appeared in his childhood vision will later become important to others. Allah’s will prevails, though many people do not know it. The story shows that hidden events can unfold toward an outcome beyond the intentions of those involved.

phrases.translation: And when he reached maturity, We gave him wisdom and knowledge. This is how We reward the good-doers
phrases.explanation: When Joseph reaches maturity, Allah grants him wisdom and knowledge. His abilities are gifts that prepare him for responsibility, not proof that he is independent of Allah. Allah rewards those who do good. Joseph’s development is presented as part of a broader pattern in which sincere conduct is met with divine favor.

phrases.translation: And the lady, in whose house he lived, tried to seduce him. She locked the doors ˹firmly˺ and said, “Come to me!” He replied, “Allah is my refuge!
phrases.explanation: The woman in whose house Joseph lives tries to seduce him and locks the doors. The closed room increases the pressure, but Joseph must still decide how to respond. Joseph seeks refuge in Allah and refuses her invitation. His response shows that awareness of Allah can guide a person when private temptation is strong.

phrases.translation: It is ˹not right to betray˺ my master, who has taken good care of me. Indeed, the wrongdoers never succeed.”
phrases.explanation: Joseph also points to the trust of the man who cared for him. Betraying that protection would be unjust as well as disobedient to Allah. Joseph says wrongdoers do not succeed. The statement connects his refusal with a wider moral truth that wrongdoing cannot secure a good final outcome.

phrases.translation: She advanced towards him, and he would have done likewise, had he not seen a sign from his Lord.
phrases.explanation: The woman advances, and Joseph would have responded likewise if he had not seen a sign from his Lord. The verse presents divine guidance as the barrier that turns him away from the temptation.

phrases.translation: This is how We kept evil and indecency away from him, for he was truly one of Our chosen servants
phrases.explanation: Allah keeps evil and indecency away from Joseph. The protection is linked to his sincere devotion rather than to a claim that he faced no pressure. Joseph is one of Allah’s chosen servants. The verse describes his character and protection in the middle of a difficult test.

phrases.translation: They raced for the door and she tore his shirt from the back,
phrases.explanation: Joseph and the woman race to the door, and his shirt is torn from behind. The direction of the tear supports the account that he was trying to escape from her.

phrases.translation: only to find her husband at the door. She cried, “What is the penalty for someone who tried to violate your wife, except imprisonment or a painful punishment?”
phrases.explanation: Her husband is standing at the door when they arrive. His unexpected presence shifts the private encounter into a question of evidence and responsibility. The woman accuses Joseph and asks for imprisonment or painful punishment. Her claim reverses what happened and attempts to make the fleeing person appear guilty.

phrases.translation: Joseph responded, “It was she who tried to seduce me.” And a witness from her own family testified: “If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth and he is a liar
phrases.explanation: Joseph states that the woman tried to seduce him. His account directly challenges her accusation and makes the truth of the incident a question to be examined. A witness from her family proposes using the shirt’s tear as evidence. If it is torn from the front, her account is supported and Joseph is lying, the witness says.

phrases.translation: But if it is torn from the back, then she has lied and he is truthful.”
phrases.explanation: If Joseph’s shirt is torn from behind, the witness says the woman has lied and Joseph is truthful. The test relies on the direction of the tear to distinguish escape from attack.

phrases.translation: So when her husband saw that Joseph’s shirt was torn from the back, he said ˹to her˺, “This must be ˹an example˺ of the cunning of you ˹women˺! Indeed, your cunning is so shrewd
phrases.explanation: Seeing the shirt torn from behind, the husband recognizes the woman’s cunning in this incident. His remark is a reaction to the evidence before him, not a reason to generalize suspicion to all women.

phrases.translation: O Joseph! Forget about this. And you ˹O wife˺! Seek forgiveness for your sin. It certainly has been your fault.”
phrases.explanation: Joseph is told to put the incident aside. The instruction ends the immediate confrontation and signals that the household does not intend to pursue him as the guilty party. The woman is told to seek forgiveness because the fault was hers. The response acknowledges her wrongdoing and directs her toward repentance rather than denying what happened.

phrases.translation: Some women of the city gossiped, “The Chief Minister’s wife is trying to seduce her slave-boy. Love for him has plagued her heart. Indeed, we see that she is clearly mistaken.”
phrases.explanation: Women in the city gossip that the Chief Minister’s wife is trying to seduce Joseph. Their talk spreads a private matter through public judgment. They say love for Joseph has overwhelmed her and judge her mistaken. Their words may reflect concern, but they also turn her situation into gossip. They claim she is clearly mistaken. The verse shows how quickly public opinion forms around the story, before the women understand its full circumstances.

phrases.translation: When she heard about their gossip, she invited them and set a banquet for them. She gave each one a knife, then said ˹to Joseph˺, “Come out before them.”
phrases.explanation: After hearing the gossip, the woman invites the critics and prepares a banquet. She brings them into the situation so they can see what has prompted her conduct. She gives each guest a knife and calls Joseph out. The arrangement sets up a startling reaction when they see him.

phrases.translation: When they saw him, they were so stunned ˹by his beauty˺ that they cut their hands, and exclaimed, “Good God! This cannot be human; this must be a noble angel!”
phrases.explanation: The women are so stunned by Joseph’s appearance that they cut their hands. Their reaction shows that the gossiping women now understand the strength of the attraction they had criticized. They exclaim that Joseph cannot be an ordinary human and call him a noble angel. Their speech conveys amazement, not a literal claim that Joseph is an angel.

phrases.translation: She said, “This is the one for whose love you criticized me! I did try to seduce him but he ˹firmly˺ refused.
phrases.explanation: The woman identifies Joseph as the one for whom the guests criticized her. She uses their reaction to defend her earlier desire rather than acknowledge that he refused. She admits that she tried to seduce Joseph and that he firmly refused. Her admission confirms his earlier account of what happened.

phrases.translation: And if he does not do what I order him to, he will certainly be imprisoned and ˹fully˺ disgraced.”
phrases.explanation: She threatens to imprison and disgrace him if he does not obey her. The threat reveals the power she can exercise in the household and the pressure Joseph continues to face.

phrases.translation: Joseph prayed, “My Lord! I would rather be in jail than do what they invite me to. And if You do not turn their cunning away from me, I might yield to them and fall into ignorance.”
phrases.explanation: Joseph asks Allah for prison rather than submitting to the wrongdoing being demanded of him. His prayer prioritizes obedience over comfort or social advancement. He asks Allah to turn the women’s cunning away from him. Joseph recognizes that he needs divine help to withstand the pressure around him. Without Allah’s protection, Joseph fears he could yield and act ignorantly. His prayer expresses humility about human vulnerability rather than confidence in his own strength alone.

phrases.translation: So his Lord responded to him, turning their cunning away from him. Surely He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing
phrases.explanation: Allah responds to Joseph by turning their cunning away from him. The verse affirms that his prayer is heard and that Allah knows the pressure and circumstances he faces fully.

phrases.translation: And so it occurred to those in charge, despite seeing all the proofs ˹of his innocence˺, that he should be imprisoned for a while
phrases.explanation: Those in charge see evidence that Joseph is innocent, yet decide to imprison him for a time. The verse shows that a correct finding does not always lead powerful people to act justly. Joseph is held in prison despite the proofs. His confinement becomes another unexpected stage in a story whose outcome is not controlled by the officials.

phrases.translation: And two other servants went to jail with Joseph. One of them said, “I dreamt I was pressing wine.” The other said, “I dreamt I was carrying ˹some˺ bread on my head, from which birds were eating.”
phrases.explanation: One prisoner dreams of pressing grapes for wine. He shares the vision with Joseph, hoping that its meaning can be understood. The other prisoner dreams of carrying bread that birds eat from his head. The two different images prompt them to seek Joseph’s interpretation.

phrases.translation: ˹Then both said,˺ “Tell us their interpretation, for we surely see you as one of the good-doers.”
phrases.explanation: Both prisoners ask Joseph to interpret their dreams. They turn to him because they see him as a person who does good, not merely as another inmate. They describe Joseph as one of the good-doers. Their confidence in his character opens the way for him to speak about the source of his knowledge.

phrases.translation: Joseph replied, “I can even tell you what kind of meal you will be served before you receive it.
phrases.explanation: Joseph says he can tell the prisoners what meal they will receive before it arrives. He presents this knowledge as a gift from Allah, not as magic or personal power.

phrases.translation: This ˹knowledge˺ is from what my Lord has taught me. I have shunned the faith of a people who disbelieve in Allah and deny the Hereafter
phrases.explanation: Joseph explains that Allah has taught him. Before interpreting their dreams, he points the prisoners toward the source of his knowledge. Joseph has left the faith of people who disbelieve in Allah and deny the Hereafter. His account of the dream is connected with a clear commitment to worship and judgment.

phrases.translation: I follow the faith of my fathers: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. It is not ˹right˺ for us to associate anything with Allah ˹in worship˺. This is part of Allah’s grace upon us and humanity, but most people are not grateful
phrases.explanation: Joseph follows the faith of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He presents his belief as continuous with the teachings of his forefathers, not as an isolated invention. Associating partners with Allah is rejected, and Joseph calls monotheism a grace upon his family and humanity. Guidance is a gift that offers people a way to worship rightly. Most people are not grateful for this grace. Joseph’s words invite his fellow prisoners to recognize the gift rather than take guidance for granted.

phrases.translation: O my fellow-prisoners! Which is far better: many different lords or Allah—the One, the Supreme
phrases.explanation: Joseph asks his fellow prisoners to compare many different lords with the One God. The question challenges the confusion and dependence created by worshipping multiple powers. Allah is the One and Supreme. Joseph’s description presents Him as uniquely worthy of worship and authority, unlike the competing lords people imagine.

phrases.translation: Whatever ˹idols˺ you worship instead of Him are mere names which you and your forefathers have made up—a practice Allah has never authorized.
phrases.explanation: The idols are only names invented by people and their forefathers. Joseph challenges the idea that a label or inherited custom can create real divine authority. Allah has never authorized this worship of idols. The verse warns against attributing religious legitimacy to a practice without revelation.

phrases.translation: It is only Allah Who decides. He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the upright faith, but most people do not know
phrases.explanation: Allah alone decides religious authority and commands that people worship none but Him. The statement directs the prisoners away from invented gods toward the true source of guidance. Worshipping Allah alone is the upright faith, though most people do not know. Joseph concludes by inviting his companions to recognize the truth and its practical claim on them.

phrases.translation: “O my fellow-prisoners! ˹The first˺ one of you will serve wine to his master, and the other will be crucified and the birds will eat from his head. The matter about which you inquired has been decided.”
phrases.explanation: Joseph tells one prisoner he will return to serving his master with wine. The dream’s interpretation gives the man a future outside prison. The other prisoner will be crucified, and birds will eat from his head. Joseph interprets the dreams honestly, even when one outcome is frightening. Joseph says the matter has been decided. He presents the interpretation as knowledge of an outcome, not as a prediction he can change by wish.

phrases.translation: Then he said to the one he knew would survive, “Mention me in the presence of your master.” But Satan made him forget to mention Joseph to his master, so he remained in prison for several years
phrases.explanation: Joseph asks the prisoner who will survive to mention him to the king. After years of confinement, he hopes that the man’s return may bring his case to attention. Satan makes the man forget to mention Joseph to the king. The missed opportunity delays Joseph’s release, even though his fate is not outside Allah’s knowledge. Joseph remains in prison for several years. The delay highlights his patience and shows that a just outcome may take time to appear.

phrases.translation: And ˹one day˺ the King said, “I dreamt of seven fat cows eaten up by seven skinny ones; and seven green ears of grain and ˹seven˺ others dry. O chiefs! Tell me the meaning of my dream if you can interpret dreams.”
phrases.explanation: The king dreams of seven fat cows eaten by seven thin ones, along with green and dry ears of grain. He asks his chiefs to interpret the vision, making a private dream a matter of public concern.

phrases.translation: They replied, “These are confused visions and we do not know the interpretation of such dreams.”
phrases.explanation: The chiefs call the dream confused visions and admit that they cannot interpret it. Their inability creates an opening for the prisoner who remembers Joseph’s skill. The king’s household cannot interpret it, while Joseph will later provide the needed understanding.

phrases.translation: ˹Finally,˺ the surviving ex-prisoner remembered ˹Joseph˺ after a long time and said, “I will tell you its interpretation, so send me forth ˹to Joseph˺.”
phrases.explanation: After a long time, the surviving former prisoner remembers Joseph and offers to seek his interpretation. The forgotten request is finally renewed when the king’s dream makes Joseph’s knowledge needed.

phrases.translation: ˹He said,˺ “Joseph, O man of truth! Interpret for us ˹the dream of˺ seven fat cows eaten up by seven skinny ones; and seven green ears of grain and ˹seven˺ others dry, so that I may return to the people and let them know.”
phrases.explanation: The former prisoner addresses Joseph as a man of truth and asks him to interpret the king’s dream. He plans to return with the answer so that the people can understand what the vision means.

phrases.translation: Joseph replied, “You will plant ˹grain˺ for seven consecutive years, leaving in the ear whatever you will harvest, except for the little you will eat
phrases.explanation: Joseph advises the people to plant grain for seven years and leave most of the harvest in its ears, eating only a little. His plan prepares them to preserve food while it is abundant.

phrases.translation: Then after that will come seven years of great hardship which will consume whatever you have saved, except the little you will store ˹for seed˺
phrases.explanation: Joseph predicts seven hard years that will consume most of what they stored. He tells them to keep a small reserve for seed, so that planting can continue through the shortage.

phrases.translation: Then after that will come a year in which people will receive abundant rain and they will press ˹oil and wine˺.”
phrases.explanation: After the years of hardship, an abundant year will bring rain and allow people to press produce. Joseph’s interpretation includes recovery as well as famine, giving the king a plan for the full cycle.

phrases.translation: The King ˹then˺ said, “Bring him to me.” When the messenger came to him, Joseph said, “Go back to your master and ask him about the case of the women who cut their hands. Surely my Lord has ˹full˺ knowledge of their cunning.”
phrases.explanation: The king orders Joseph to be brought before him. The opportunity to leave prison arrives after Joseph has interpreted the dream and offered a useful plan. Joseph asks the messenger to return and have the women’s case investigated before he comes out. He wants the truth about the earlier accusation made clear, rather than leaving prison under a cloud of suspicion.

phrases.translation: The King asked ˹the women˺, “What did you get when you tried to seduce Joseph?” They replied, “Allah forbid! We know nothing indecent about him.”
phrases.explanation: The king asks the women what happened when they tried to seduce Joseph. His question gives them an opportunity to speak about the incident openly. The women deny knowing anything indecent about Joseph. Their answer supports his innocence rather than repeating the accusation made earlier.

phrases.translation: Then the Chief Minister’s wife admitted, “Now the truth has come to light. It was I who tried to seduce him, and he is surely truthful
phrases.explanation: The Chief Minister’s wife admits that she tried to seduce Joseph and says he is truthful. The truth is now stated publicly by the person who had made the false accusation.

phrases.translation: From this, Joseph should know that I did not speak dishonestly about him in his absence, for Allah certainly does not guide the scheming of the dishonest
phrases.explanation: The speaker says Joseph should know that no dishonest statement was made about him in his absence, and that Allah does not guide dishonest scheming. The words emphasize truthfulness and accountability even when the person harmed is not present.

phrases.translation: And I do not seek to free myself from blame, for indeed the soul is ever inclined to evil, except those shown mercy by my Lord. Surely my Lord is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”
phrases.explanation: The statement acknowledges that the soul can incline toward evil unless Allah shows mercy. It rejects self-righteousness and places hope in Allah’s forgiveness and compassion. A person should ask for mercy rather than assume they are beyond temptation.

phrases.translation: The King said, “Bring him to me. I will employ him exclusively in my service.” And when Joseph spoke to him, the King said, “Today you are highly esteemed and fully trusted by us.”
phrases.explanation: The king asks for Joseph and says he will employ him exclusively. His dream interpretation and careful conduct have made the king want to give him a position of responsibility. After speaking with Joseph, the king calls him highly esteemed and fully trusted. Joseph’s release is accompanied by public recognition of his reliability.

phrases.translation: Joseph proposed, “Put me in charge of the store-houses of the land, for I am truly reliable and adept.”
phrases.explanation: Joseph asks to oversee the storehouses of the land, describing himself as reliable and adept. The request places his proven ability in service of managing the resources the country will need.

phrases.translation: This is how We established Joseph in the land to settle wherever he pleased. We shower Our mercy on whoever We will, and We never discount the reward of the good-doers
phrases.explanation: Allah establishes Joseph in the land, where he can settle as he chooses. The verse attributes his new security and authority to Allah’s mercy and reminds readers that good-doers are never denied their reward.

phrases.translation: And the reward of the Hereafter is far better for those who are faithful and are mindful ˹of Allah˺
phrases.explanation: The reward of the Hereafter is far better than worldly position for those who believe and remain mindful of Allah. Joseph’s success in this life does not replace the greater lasting reward.

phrases.translation: And Joseph’s brothers came and entered his presence. He recognized them but they were unaware of who he really was
phrases.explanation: Joseph’s brothers arrive and enter his presence. He recognizes them, but they do not recognize him, creating a reversal in their relationship that they cannot yet see. His changed status gives him the chance to meet them again.

phrases.translation: When he had provided them with their supplies, he demanded, “Bring me your brother on your father’s side. Do you not see that I give full measure and I am the best of hosts
phrases.explanation: After providing their supplies, Joseph asks his brothers to bring their younger brother from their father. The request begins the next stage of the family story and reflects the household Joseph remembers. Joseph reminds them that he gives full measure and is a good host. His treatment of them is generous, even though they do not know who he is.

phrases.translation: But if you do not bring him to me ˹next time˺, I will have no grain for you, nor will you ever come close to me again.”
phrases.explanation: Joseph warns that if they do not bring their brother next time, they will receive no grain and cannot approach him again. The condition gives them a strong reason to return with the family member he has requested.

phrases.translation: They promised, “We will try to convince his father to let him come. We will certainly do ˹our best˺.”
phrases.explanation: Joseph’s brothers promise to try to persuade their father and say they will do their best. Their words indicate a willingness to return with Benjamin, though Jacob will require a solemn guarantee.

phrases.translation: Joseph ordered his servants to put his brothers’ money back into their saddlebags so that they would find it when they returned to their family and perhaps they would come back
phrases.explanation: Joseph orders his servants to return the brothers’ money to their bags. He wants them to find it when they reach home, which may encourage them to come back. Joseph hopes the returned money will bring the brothers back. His plan quietly creates a reason for another journey without revealing his identity.

phrases.translation: When Joseph’s brothers returned to their father, they pleaded, “O our father! We have been denied ˹further˺ supplies. So send our brother with us so that we may receive our measure, and we will definitely watch over him.”
phrases.explanation: The brothers tell Jacob that they have been denied more supplies. The statement adds urgency to their request to bring Benjamin on the next trip. They ask to take Benjamin so the family can receive its ration. They promise to watch over him, repeating the assurance they had given before Joseph disappeared. Their promise must now be weighed against their past betrayal. Jacob has reason to be cautious even though the family needs food.

phrases.translation: He responded, “Should I trust you with him as I once trusted you with his brother ˹Joseph˺? But ˹only˺ Allah is the best Protector, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful.”
phrases.explanation: Jacob recalls that he once trusted the brothers with Joseph. His question shows why he cannot accept their new promise without remembering what happened before. Jacob says Allah is the best Protector and the Most Merciful. He recognizes that human promises can fail and places his ultimate trust in Allah.

phrases.translation: When they opened their bags, they discovered that their money had been returned to them. They argued, “O our father! What more can we ask for? Here is our money, fully returned to us.
phrases.explanation: The brothers find that their money has been returned. They treat this unexpected benefit as a reason to persuade Jacob to let them travel again. They ask what more they could want, emphasizing that their payment has come back. The money makes their request more persuasive to the family.

phrases.translation: Now we can buy more food for our family. We will watch over our brother, and obtain an extra camel-load of grain. That load can be easily secured.”
phrases.explanation: They explain that they can use the money to buy more food for everyone at home. Their appeal combines practical need with a promise to care for Benjamin. They promise to watch over Benjamin and obtain an extra camel-load of grain. The offer is meant to secure Jacob’s agreement by showing both family benefit and personal care.

phrases.translation: Jacob insisted, “I will not send him with you until you give me a solemn oath by Allah that you will certainly bring him back to me, unless you are totally overpowered.”
phrases.explanation: Jacob refuses to send Benjamin until the brothers swear by Allah that they will bring him back, unless they are overwhelmed beyond their control. The oath sets a solemn condition.

phrases.translation: Then after they had given him their oaths, he concluded, “Allah is a Witness to what we have said.”
phrases.explanation: After the brothers take the oath, Jacob says Allah is witness to their words. The reminder makes their promise answerable not only to their father but to Allah. Jacob’s caution reflects his painful experience with Joseph. He accepts the journey only after the brothers make a binding commitment.

phrases.translation: He then instructed ˹them˺, “O my sons! Do not enter ˹the city˺ all through one gate, but through separate gates. I cannot help you against ˹what is destined by˺ Allah in the least.
phrases.explanation: Jacob tells his sons to enter the city through separate gates rather than together. The precaution reflects his concern for their safety in a place where they are strangers. He admits that his advice cannot protect them against Allah’s decree. Human precautions have a place, but they do not control what Allah decides.

phrases.translation: It is only Allah Who decides. In Him I put my trust. And in Him let the faithful put their trust.”
phrases.explanation: Jacob says that Allah alone decides and that he trusts in Him. He combines reasonable caution with reliance on Allah rather than treating either as a substitute for the other. The faithful are also told to put their trust in Allah. Jacob’s example is offered as a model of reliance for believers facing uncertainty.

phrases.translation: Then when they entered as their father had instructed them, this did not help them against ˹the Will of˺ Allah whatsoever. It was just a desire in Jacob’s heart which he satisfied.
phrases.explanation: The brothers follow Jacob’s instructions, but their separate entry cannot change Allah’s will. The verse distinguishes taking sensible precautions from assuming that they determine the outcome. Jacob’s instruction satisfies a desire in his heart. It is a father’s effort to protect his sons, even though it cannot override the decree of Allah.

phrases.translation: He was truly blessed with ˹great˺ knowledge because of what We had taught him, but most people have no knowledge
phrases.explanation: Jacob has knowledge because Allah taught him. The verse attributes his understanding to divine instruction rather than presenting it as independent foresight. Most people do not know. The conclusion reminds readers that the relationship between human effort and Allah’s decree may not be fully visible to them.

phrases.translation: When they entered Joseph’s presence, he called his brother ˹Benjamin˺ aside, and confided ˹to him˺, “I am indeed your brother ˹Joseph˺! So do not feel distressed about what they have been doing.”
phrases.explanation: Joseph takes Benjamin aside and reveals his identity. The secret meeting gives his younger brother reassurance after the years of separation and uncertainty. Joseph tells Benjamin not to grieve over what the brothers have done. He offers comfort while keeping his identity hidden from the others for the time being.

phrases.translation: When Joseph had provided them with supplies, he slipped the royal cup into his brother’s bag. Then a herald cried, “O people of the caravan! You must be thieves!”
phrases.explanation: Joseph first provides his brothers with supplies. His generosity continues even as he prepares a plan that will keep Benjamin with him. Joseph has the royal measuring cup placed in Benjamin’s bag. This is part of the plan that creates a reason to detain his brother, not an action the brothers understand at the time. A herald accuses the caravan of theft. The announcement turns the travelers back and begins the search for the missing cup.

phrases.translation: They asked, turning back, “What have you lost?”
phrases.explanation: The brothers turn around and ask what has been lost. Their question responds to the herald’s accusation and gives the officials an opportunity to state the charge. They have not yet been told where the cup might be.

phrases.translation: The herald ˹along with the guards˺ replied, “We have lost the King’s measuring cup. And whoever brings it will be awarded a camel-load ˹of grain˺. I guarantee it.”
phrases.explanation: The herald says that the king’s measuring cup is missing. Identifying the object explains why the caravan has been stopped and searched. A camel-load of grain is promised to whoever returns the cup. The reward gives the search an incentive and connects the missing object with the brothers’ urgent need for food. The herald guarantees the reward. His statement presents the offer as a definite promise, not an uncertain possibility.

phrases.translation: Joseph’s brothers replied, “By Allah! You know well that we did not come to cause trouble in the land, nor are we thieves.”
phrases.explanation: Joseph’s brothers swear that they came neither to cause trouble nor to steal. They defend their reputation and insist that the accusation does not match their conduct. Their denial sets out the conduct they claim to have maintained.

phrases.translation: Joseph’s men asked, “What should be the price for theft, if you are lying?”
phrases.explanation: Joseph’s men ask what penalty should apply if the brothers are lying. The question invites them to state their own standard for theft before the search identifies anyone. The question tests whether their proposed penalty matches their own standard.

phrases.translation: Joseph’s brothers responded, “The price will be ˹the enslavement of˺ the one in whose bag the cup is found. That is how we punish the wrongdoers.”
phrases.explanation: The brothers say that the person whose bag contains the cup should be taken. They describe this as their way of punishing wrongdoers, not yet knowing that the cup has been placed in Benjamin’s bag.

phrases.translation: Joseph began searching their bags before that of his brother ˹Benjamin˺, then brought it out of Benjamin’s bag.
phrases.explanation: Joseph searches the other bags before Benjamin’s. The order ensures that the cup is not found too early and reveals the plan only when Benjamin’s bag is examined. The cup is found in Benjamin’s bag. The discovery gives Joseph a way to keep his brother, while the brothers believe the search has uncovered a theft.

phrases.translation: This is how We inspired Joseph to plan. He could not have taken his brother under the King’s law, but Allah had so willed. We elevate in rank whoever We will. But above those ranking in knowledge is the One All-Knowing
phrases.explanation: Allah inspires Joseph’s plan, since Joseph could not keep his brother under the king’s law. The verse distinguishes the legal rule in Egypt from the outcome Allah has enabled. Allah wills to elevate people in rank, and above every person of knowledge is the All-Knowing. Human understanding is limited beside Allah’s complete knowledge.

phrases.translation: ˹To distance themselves,˺ Joseph’s brothers argued, “If he has stolen, so did his ˹full˺ brother before.” But Joseph suppressed his outrage—revealing nothing to them—and said ˹to himself˺, “You are in such an evil position, and Allah knows best ˹the truth of˺ what you claim.”
phrases.explanation: The brothers claim that if Benjamin stole, Joseph must have stolen before him. Their accusation repeats an old family resentment and attempts to distance themselves from Benjamin. Joseph suppresses his anger and reveals nothing. He recognizes the brothers’ words as deeply wrong but keeps control of his response. Joseph says Allah knows the truth of their claim. He leaves the hidden facts to Allah rather than disclosing his identity in the heat of the moment.

phrases.translation: They appealed, “O Chief Minister! He has a very old father, so take one of us instead. We surely see you as one of the good-doers.”
phrases.explanation: The brothers plead that their father is very old and ask Joseph to take one of them instead. They appeal to his kindness, hoping he will release Benjamin from the consequence they have described.

phrases.translation: Joseph responded, “Allah forbid that we should take other than the one with whom we found our property. Otherwise, we would surely be unjust.”
phrases.explanation: Joseph refuses to take anyone other than the person in whose bag the cup was found. He says doing so would be unjust, applying the rule the brothers themselves had stated.

phrases.translation: When they lost all hope in him, they spoke privately. The eldest of them said, “Do you not know that your father had taken a solemn oath by Allah from you, nor how you failed him regarding Joseph before?
phrases.explanation: When Joseph refuses, the brothers lose hope and confer in private. Their discussion turns from trying to persuade the official to facing the promise they made to their father. The eldest brother reminds them of Jacob’s solemn oath and their earlier failure concerning Joseph. The past makes their current predicament especially painful.

phrases.translation: So I am not leaving this land until my father allows me to, or Allah decides for me. For He is the Best of Judges
phrases.explanation: He refuses to leave until their father permits him or Allah decides otherwise. His decision reflects responsibility for the oath and the shame of repeating an earlier betrayal. He trusts Allah as the Best of Judges. The statement leaves the final resolution to Allah rather than assuming the brothers can repair everything by themselves.

phrases.translation: Return to your father and say, ‘O our father! Your son committed theft.
phrases.explanation: The brothers are instructed to tell Jacob that Benjamin was found with the missing cup and is being held. They present the event as a theft, following the rule they themselves had stated.

phrases.translation: We testify only to what we know. We could not guard against the unforeseen
phrases.explanation: They say they can testify only to what they witnessed. Their statement limits their claim and prepares the father to verify the account for himself. They add that they could not guard against the unforeseen. The phrase acknowledges that events exceeded their control, though Jacob will remember their earlier failure with Joseph.

phrases.translation: Ask ˹the people of˺ the land where we were and the caravan we travelled with. We are certainly telling the truth.’”
phrases.explanation: The brothers invite Jacob to ask the people of the land and the caravan that travelled with them. They want outside witnesses to confirm that the story is not invented. They insist that they are telling the truth. Their confidence in the account contrasts with the deception they practiced in the earlier episode with Joseph.

phrases.translation: He cried, “No! Your souls must have tempted you to do something ˹evil˺. So ˹I am left with nothing but˺ beautiful patience!
phrases.explanation: Jacob again says that the brothers’ souls tempted them to do evil. He does not accept their story without question, remembering the earlier betrayal that shaped his grief. Jacob chooses beautiful patience once more. This does not mean he feels no sorrow, but that he will bear it without abandoning faith or turning to wrongdoing.

phrases.translation: I trust Allah will return them all to me. Surely He ˹alone˺ is the All-Knowing, All-Wise.”
phrases.explanation: Jacob trusts that Allah may return all his sons to him. His hope extends beyond Benjamin to Joseph, whom he has mourned for many years. Allah is All-Knowing and All-Wise. Jacob relies on divine knowledge and wisdom when he cannot see how the family’s losses will be resolved.

phrases.translation: He turned away from them, lamenting, “Alas, poor Joseph!” And his eyes turned white out of the grief he suppressed
phrases.explanation: Jacob turns away and grieves for Joseph again. Benjamin’s absence reopens an old sorrow, showing how deeply the earlier separation continues to affect him. His eyes turn white from the grief he suppresses. The physical description conveys the intensity of his loss, while he continues to endure it patiently.

phrases.translation: They said, “By Allah! You will not cease to remember Joseph until you lose your health or ˹even˺ your life.”
phrases.explanation: The sons tell Jacob he will keep remembering Joseph until grief ruins his health or kills him. Their words show that they do not understand the depth of his attachment or the hope he still holds.

phrases.translation: He replied, “I complain of my anguish and sorrow only to Allah, and I know from Allah what you do not know
phrases.explanation: Jacob says he complains of his anguish and sorrow only to Allah. Turning to Allah with grief is compatible with patience and gives him a place to express what he carries. Jacob knows from Allah what his sons do not know. His confidence rests on revelation and hope in Allah, even when the family cannot yet see what will happen.

phrases.translation: O my sons! Go and search ˹diligently˺ for Joseph and his brother. And do not lose hope in the mercy of Allah, for no one loses hope in Allah’s mercy except those with no faith.”
phrases.explanation: Jacob sends his sons to search diligently for Joseph and Benjamin. The instruction shows that he has not given up on finding either of them. He tells them not to lose hope in Allah’s mercy. Their difficult circumstances do not place them beyond the possibility of relief and forgiveness. Only those without faith lose hope in Allah’s mercy. The verse treats despair as a failure to trust Allah’s compassion, not as an unavoidable response to grief.

phrases.translation: When they entered Joseph’s presence, they pleaded, “O Chief Minister! We and our family have been touched with hardship, and we have brought only a few worthless coins, but ˹please˺ give us our supplies in full and be charitable to us. Indeed, Allah rewards the charitable.”
phrases.explanation: The brothers describe the hardship facing their family and say they have brought only a small payment. Their appeal asks Joseph to consider their difficult circumstances. They ask for their full measure and appeal for charity. Their request combines the need to feed their family with a plea for generosity beyond what they can pay. They remind Joseph that Allah rewards the charitable. The words appeal to compassion and encourage generosity toward people in need.

phrases.translation: He asked, “Do you remember what you did to Joseph and his brother in your ignorance?”
phrases.explanation: Joseph asks whether they remember what they did to him and Benjamin when they acted ignorantly. The question begins to reveal that he knows their history and invites them to face it.

phrases.translation: They replied ˹in shock˺, “Are you really Joseph?” He said, “I am Joseph, and here is my brother ˹Benjamin˺! Allah has truly been gracious to us.
phrases.explanation: The brothers are shocked and ask whether the Chief Minister is truly Joseph. Recognition changes their position from petitioners before a stranger to people confronting the brother they betrayed. Joseph identifies Benjamin and credits Allah with being gracious to the family. Their reunion is framed as a blessing, not as Joseph’s personal triumph over his brothers.

phrases.translation: Surely whoever is mindful ˹of Allah˺ and patient, then certainly Allah never discounts the reward of the good-doers.”
phrases.explanation: Joseph says that mindfulness of Allah and patience are followed by reward. His own story shows why restraint and trust matter even through long hardship. Allah never reduces the reward of those who do good. The statement reassures the brothers and draws a general lesson from the family’s experience.

phrases.translation: They admitted, “By Allah! Allah has truly preferred you over us, and we have surely been sinful.”
phrases.explanation: The brothers admit that Allah preferred Joseph over them and that they were sinful. Their confession replaces earlier accusations and begins an honest acknowledgment of the harm they caused. This admission opens a path to reconciliation.

phrases.translation: Joseph said, “There is no blame on you today. May Allah forgive you! He is the Most Merciful of the merciful
phrases.explanation: Joseph tells his brothers that he will not blame them today. He chooses reconciliation rather than using his new authority to punish them for their earlier betrayal. Joseph asks Allah to forgive his brothers. Forgiveness is directed to Allah, whose mercy can address wrongdoing more fully than revenge can. Allah is the Most Merciful of the merciful. Joseph ends with hope in divine compassion rather than in the power he now holds over his family.

phrases.translation: Go with this shirt of mine and cast it over my father’s face,
phrases.explanation: Joseph gives his brothers his shirt and tells them to place it over Jacob’s face. The garment carries a sign that can restore hope to the father who has grieved for him.

phrases.translation: and he will regain his sight. Then come back to me with your whole family.”
phrases.explanation: Jacob will regain his sight when the shirt is placed over his face. The moment links the family’s reunion with the healing of a grief that had affected him physically. Joseph asks his brothers to return with the whole family. The reunion is now close enough that the family can travel together to Egypt.

phrases.translation: When the caravan departed ˹from Egypt˺, their father said ˹to those around him˺, “You may think I am senile, but I certainly sense the smell of Joseph.”
phrases.explanation: As the caravan leaves Egypt, Jacob senses the smell of Joseph. His words reveal a continuing hope that the lost son is alive and that the separation may end. Those around Jacob think he is senile, but he insists that he senses Joseph. Their doubt contrasts with the knowledge and hope Jacob holds from Allah.

phrases.translation: They replied, “By Allah! You are definitely still in your old delusion.”
phrases.explanation: The people around Jacob say he remains in his old delusion. They interpret his certainty as confusion because they do not know that Joseph is alive and nearby. Their response shows how hope can be misunderstood when others do not know the hidden facts.

phrases.translation: But when the bearer of the good news arrived, he cast the shirt over Jacob’s face, so he regained his sight. Jacob then said ˹to his children˺, “Did I not tell you that I truly know from Allah what you do not know?”
phrases.explanation: The bearer of good news arrives and places Joseph’s shirt over Jacob’s face, restoring his sight. The sign confirms that Jacob’s long hope was not misplaced. Jacob reminds his children that he knew from Allah what they did not know. His earlier patience and hope are vindicated when the promised reunion becomes visible.

phrases.translation: They begged, “O our father! Pray for the forgiveness of our sins. We have certainly been sinful.”
phrases.explanation: The brothers ask Jacob to pray for forgiveness for their sins. They now admit that their actions were sinful and seek help in turning back to Allah. They now admit their wrongdoing and ask that it be forgiven.

phrases.translation: He said, “I will pray to my Lord for your forgiveness. He ˹alone˺ is indeed the All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”
phrases.explanation: Jacob promises to ask his Lord to forgive the brothers. His response accepts their repentance and directs their hope toward Allah’s mercy. Allah alone is All-Forgiving and Most Merciful. Jacob’s confidence in forgiveness rests on Allah’s qualities, not on the family’s ability to erase the past by itself.

phrases.translation: When they entered Joseph’s presence, he received his parents ˹graciously˺ and said, “Enter Egypt, Allah willing, in security.”
phrases.explanation: When the family enters Joseph’s presence, he welcomes his parents graciously. The reunion contrasts with his earlier separation from them and shows his care for his family. Joseph invites them to enter Egypt in security, if Allah wills. Their journey ends with safety after years of loss, famine, and uncertainty.

phrases.translation: Then he raised his parents to the throne, and they all fell down in prostration to Joseph, who then said,
phrases.explanation: Joseph raises his parents to the throne, and the family prostrates before him. In the story, this gesture of honor fulfills the dream he told his father as a child, rather than making Joseph an object of worship.

phrases.translation: “O my dear father! This is the interpretation of my old dream. My Lord has made it come true. He was truly kind to me when He freed me from prison, and brought you all from the desert after Satan had ignited rivalry between me and my siblings.
phrases.explanation: Joseph recognizes the scene as the interpretation of his childhood dream. What once seemed distant has come true through a long chain of events he could not have planned. Joseph thanks Allah for freeing him from prison and reuniting the family after Satan stirred rivalry among the brothers. He names the hardship without letting it erase gratitude for the outcome.

phrases.translation: Indeed my Lord is subtle in fulfilling what He wills. Surely He ˹alone˺ is the All-Knowing, All-Wise.”
phrases.explanation: Allah is subtle in bringing about what He wills. Events that seemed disconnected, including betrayal and imprisonment, have led to a reunion and a place of safety. Allah is All-Knowing and All-Wise. Joseph closes by recognizing that the full meaning of events was known to Allah even when the people involved could not see it.

phrases.translation: “My Lord! You have surely granted me authority and taught me the interpretation of dreams.
phrases.explanation: Joseph thanks Allah for authority and for teaching him to interpret dreams. He recognizes that both his position and knowledge are gifts from his Lord, not achievements detached from divine care.

phrases.translation: ˹O˺ Originator of the heavens and the earth! You are my Guardian in this world and the Hereafter. Allow me to die as one who submits and join me with the righteous.”
phrases.explanation: He calls Allah the Originator of the heavens and earth and his Guardian in both worlds. Joseph’s trust extends beyond his current success to the life after death. Joseph asks to die in submission to Allah. His prayer values faithful devotion at the end of life more than worldly rank or recognition. He asks to be joined with the righteous. The request expresses hope for companionship with those who remain faithful and do good.

phrases.translation: That is from the stories of the unseen which We reveal to you ˹O Prophet˺. You were not present when they ˹all˺ made up their minds, and when they plotted ˹against Joseph˺
phrases.explanation: The story is described as knowledge of the unseen revealed to the Prophet. This framing explains how he can relate events from Joseph’s life that he did not witness. The Prophet was not present when the brothers planned and plotted against Joseph. The account’s details are presented as revelation, not as information he had personally observed.

phrases.translation: And most people will not believe—no matter how keen you are—
phrases.explanation: Most people will not believe, no matter how eager the Prophet is for them to accept the message. He can invite and explain, but he cannot compel another person’s faith.

phrases.translation: even though you are not asking them for a reward for this ˹Quran˺. It is only a reminder to the whole world
phrases.explanation: The Prophet asks no payment for conveying the Quran. It is a reminder for all people, offered as guidance rather than as a service sold for personal reward. It is offered freely and should be heard thoughtfully.

phrases.translation: How many signs in the heavens and the earth do they pass by with indifference
phrases.explanation: People pass many signs in the heavens and earth without reflection. The verse criticizes indifference to evidence that surrounds them, not a shortage of signs to consider. Their passing by allows insight to go unused.

phrases.translation: And most of them do not believe in Allah without associating others with Him ˹in worship˺
phrases.explanation: Many people acknowledge Allah yet associate others with Him in worship. The verse warns that belief in Allah is not complete when devotion is divided with partners. The verse calls for undivided worship.

phrases.translation: Do they feel secure that an overwhelming torment from Allah will not overtake them, or that the Hour will not take them by surprise when they least expect ˹it˺
phrases.explanation: The verse asks whether people feel secure from an overwhelming torment sent by Allah. Their apparent safety should not be mistaken for immunity from judgment. The Hour may arrive suddenly when people least expect it. The question urges them not to delay reflection until accountability becomes impossible to ignore.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “This is my way. I invite to Allah with insight—I and those who follow me.
phrases.explanation: The Prophet describes his way as inviting people to Allah with insight. The call is based on clear understanding, not blind imitation or an attempt to gain personal power. The Prophet and his followers share this invitation. Their role is to call others toward Allah with knowledge and clarity.

phrases.translation: Glory be to Allah, and I am not one of the polytheists.”
phrases.explanation: Glory belongs to Allah, who is free of imperfection. The statement turns the invitation toward praise of the One being called to worship. The Prophet says he is not one of the polytheists. His message is grounded in worshipping Allah alone, without associating partners with Him.

phrases.translation: We only sent before you ˹O Prophet˺ men inspired by Us from among the people of each society. Have the deniers not travelled through the land to see what was the end of those ˹destroyed˺ before them?
phrases.explanation: Earlier messengers were men from among their own communities, inspired by Allah. The pattern makes the guidance accessible to people in the societies where the messengers live. The deniers are asked to travel and observe the end of earlier destroyed peoples. History offers evidence about the consequences of rejecting messengers.

phrases.translation: And surely the ˹eternal˺ Home of the Hereafter is far better for those mindful ˹of Allah˺. Will you not then understand
phrases.explanation: The eternal Home of the Hereafter is better for those who are mindful of Allah. Lasting reward outweighs the temporary gains people may protect through wrongdoing. The verse asks whether people will understand this lesson. Reflection on history and the Hereafter should lead to a change in how they live.

phrases.translation: And when the messengers despaired and their people thought the messengers had been denied help, Our help came to them ˹at last˺. We then saved whoever We willed, and Our punishment is never averted from the wicked people
phrases.explanation: The messengers reach a point of despair while their people think they will not be helped. The verse describes how severe opposition can make relief seem delayed or absent. Allah’s help eventually comes, and He saves whoever He wills. The outcome arrives at His timing, not according to the expectations of either the messengers’ opponents or their followers. Allah’s punishment is never averted from wicked people. The verse closes by distinguishing the rescue of believers from the consequence of persistent wrongdoing.

phrases.translation: In their stories there is truly a lesson for people of reason. This message cannot be a fabrication, rather ˹it is˺ a confirmation of previous revelation,
phrases.explanation: The stories of the messengers contain lessons for people who use reason. The narrative invites reflection on patience, trust, repentance, and the consequences of injustice. The message is not fabricated and confirms earlier revelation. The surah presents its stories as part of a continuing history of divine guidance.

phrases.translation: a detailed explanation of all things, a guide, and a mercy for people of faith
phrases.explanation: The Quran gives detailed explanation and guidance. It addresses people’s need for understanding and direction rather than merely relating past events. The message is a mercy for people of faith. The conclusion gathers its purposes as confirmation, explanation, guidance, and care for those who believe.
